FROM PATTERNS TO EXPLANATIONS

What can the numbers tell us?

Who is being hurt, where it happens and which questions deserve closer investigation. Explaining why needs more evidence.

The essentials, in plain English

Counts show the scale of the problem

KSI means killed or seriously injured. A group with more KSI casualties contributes more to the recorded injury burden. It may also contain more riders or cover more miles.

A percentage needs a denominator

“KSI among casualties” describes how severe the recorded injuries were. It is not the chance of crashing, or the risk per journey. Comparing that risk needs suitable mileage or other exposure data.

Age is not riding experience

A rider aged 35–44 or 65+ may be experienced, newly qualified or returning after a break. These records do not identify which. A “returning rider” explanation is a research question.

An observed rise is not an explanation

Changes can reflect riding activity, population mix, reporting and ordinary year-to-year variation. A time coincidence does not show that advice, training or technology caused a change.

What we can examine now

The existing explorer combines age and motorcycle category with these recorded circumstances. These describe events and surroundings; they are not police-assessed contributory factors.

Recorded informationUseful questionWhat it cannot establish

ADDITIONAL DATA NEEDED

Contributory factors: the next evidence to add

Not yet included in this site’s record-level analysis. Detailed contributory / road safety factors are absent from our open-data extracts. Access requires a DfT application and data-use agreement. No request has been submitted through this site.

Relevant assessments cover braking unsuitable for conditions, poor manoeuvres, observation, experience, speed, distraction and impairment. These would help us investigate rider-control and hazard-response questions. They would not supply measured reaction times or brake inputs.

We need to distinguish a factor assigned to the motorcyclist from one assigned to another participant. Several factors may apply to one collision; missing factors do not mean no contributing problems existed. These are police assessments, not definitive findings of causation.

The older contributory-factor system is being replaced by road safety factors. Recording changes can create apparent trends, so comparisons must account for the reporting system and police-force coverage.

DfT definitions, limitations and access arrangements · Published summary tables

What might explain the age patterns?

Possible explanationEvidence needed to test it
More riding in particular age groupsAge-specific mileage, rider numbers and trip patterns
Returning after a riding breakRiding history, time away, recent mileage and familiarisation
Different motorcycles or unfamiliar controlsVerified model, safety-system fitment, ownership history and rider familiarity
Braking, observation or avoidance difficultiesParticipant-linked factors and instrumented tests of braking, steering and response time
Effects of advice or trainingWho received it, when, changes in behaviour and suitable comparison groups

These are hypotheses, not findings that any particular organisation, training approach or technology caused casualties.

How certain are the changes?

The recorded counts are the observed totals. Statistical intervals describe variation under a model; they do not fix missing records or biased reporting. Wide intervals mean the data leave substantial uncertainty about the underlying change.

The age table now shows individual 95% uncertainty intervals and tests adjusted for examining multiple age groups. A ratio of 1 means unchanged counts; 1.5 means a 50% rise. A result that does not meet a statistical threshold can still warrant investigation, and a result that does meet it does not establish a cause.

Research priorities

  1. Use age, capacity and recorded circumstances to define focused questions.
  2. Obtain participant-linked factor data through DfT and check coverage and recording changes.
  3. Collect riding histories to distinguish returning riders from continuous riders.
  4. Use controlled, instrumented studies to measure braking into turns, hazard avoidance and cue-to-action response time.
